talks.speaker: Alane Suhr
talks.title: Language Use and Learning in Embodied Interactions
talks.abstract: The natural habitat of language is interaction between human language-users contemporaneously situated in a shared environment. Modern language technologies, however, are almost exclusively built upon language outside of this context, such as text contributed to digital platforms. This approach ignores many of the phenomena fundamental to language use. Today, I will first present work on studying language use in collaborative situated games, highlighting a number of these fundamental phenomena. Then, I will highlight some recent work on building language technologies that operate in and "learn" from situated interactions.
talks.bio: Alane Suhr is an Assistant Professor at UC Berkeley EECS (with a PhD in Computer Science from Cornell University, 2022). Alane's research broadly comprises the study of language and language use (especially in situated and jointly embodied interactions, and/or interactions that comprise multiple agents), through a computational lens. In practice, This work often intersects with contemporary efforts in designing and deploying language technologies.

talks.speaker: Hale Sirin
talks.title: A Framework for Exploring In-Context Learning for Unseen Languages
talks.abstract: Recent advances in large language models have sparked growing interest in their ability to learn new languages from context alone. However, studying this capability in truly low-resource or previously unseen languages remains challenging due to the scarcity of data, tools, and evaluation benchmarks. As a result, progress is difficult to measure, experiments are often limited in scope, and findings tend to focus on only a small number of languages and tasks. In this talk, I will present a new framework that enables systematic study of in-context language learning under controlled yet realistic conditions. The key idea is to transform high-resource languages into synthetic, previously unseen variants through reversible transformations, allowing us to retain access to rich linguistic resources while simulating the challenges of low-resource settings. This approach opens the door to large-scale, reproducible experimentation that was previously infeasible.
talks.bio: Hale Sirin is an Assistant Research Professor at Johns Hopkins University and a Program Scientist at Schmidt Sciences AI and Advanced Computing Institute. Her research investigates how AI can understand language, culture, and narrative across the world’s linguistic diversity, with the goal of advancing multilingual capabilities of AI models. At Schmidt Sciences, she leads programs focused on advancing beneficial AI, including the Humanities and AI Virtual Institute and AI Agents. Previously, she was a postdoctoral fellow in computational linguistics at Johns Hopkins, focusing on AI research for cultural heritage. She holds a PhD from Johns Hopkins and an MA from the University of Chicago, and is an active member of the AI and Society research community, serving on the program committees of NLP4DH and the ACL Special Interest Group on Language Technologies for the Socio-Economic Sciences and Humanities.

talks.speaker: Ali Behrouz
talks.title: The Illusion of Deep Learning Architecture
talks.abstract: Designing efficient and effective architectural backbones as well as optimization algorithms have been in the core of research efforts to enhance the capability of foundation models. We reconceptualize neural architectures as well as optimization algorithms as associative memory modules that learn a mapping of keys and values using an internal objective, referred to as attentional bias. Surprisingly, we observed that most existing sequence models leverage either (1) dot-product similarity, or (2) L2 regression objectives as their attentional bias. Going beyond these objectives, we present a set of alternative attentional bias configurations along with their effective approximations to stabilize their training procedure. We then reinterpret forgetting mechanisms in modern deep learning architectures as a form of retention regularization, providing a novel set of forget gates for sequence models. Building upon these insights, we present Miras, a general framework to design deep learning architectures based on four choices of: (i) associative memory architecture, (ii) attentional bias objective, (iii) retention gate, and (iv) memory learning algorithm. We present novel sequence models, including Titans, Atlas, and Hope, that show exceptional performance in tasks such as language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and recall intensive tasks, even outperforming Transformers and other modern linear recurrent models.
talks.bio: I am a second-year Ph.D. student in the Computer Science Department at Cornell University, and a research intern at Google Research (NYC). Before joining Cornell, I completed my M.Sc. in Computer Science at the University of British Columbia, where I had been extremely fortunate to be advised by Prof. Margo Seltzer. Before that, I received my B.Sc. in Computer Engineering with a minor in Mathematics at the Sharif University of Technology. I am interested in a diverse topics of research and I am currently working on deep learning architectures, ML in healthcare, and computational neuroscience.

talks.speaker: Bhuwan Dhingra
talks.title: Language Models as Epistemic Interfaces: Knowledge, Agents, and Their Limits
talks.abstract: Language models are rapidly becoming the primary interface through which people consume information and delegate complex tasks. They are deployed in two increasingly dominant modes: as knowledge interfaces that synthesize answers from vast corpora, and as agents that interact with tools and environments over long horizons. Both modes offer remarkable capabilities, but both also obscure important epistemic signals in ways that become more consequential as these systems grow more trusted. In this talk, I will present recent work from my lab on understanding and improving LMs along both dimensions. On the knowledge interface side, I will introduce a retrieval-free approach to knowledge attribution that enables models to cite their pretraining data, and a framework for calibrating long-form generation where correctness and confidence are treated as distributions rather than binary outcomes. On the agentic side, I will show that coding agents are surprisingly effective long-context processors – including a strong result on ARC-AGI-3 – but also that RL-trained agents develop characteristic failure modes over long horizons that aggregate benchmarks tend to hide. I will argue that both settings face a common challenge: making the reasoning and uncertainty of these systems legible to the humans who depend on them.
talks.bio: Bhuwan Dhingra is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Duke University and a Research Scientist at Apple. He has also spent time at Google DeepMind as part of the post-training team for the Gemini foundation models. His research focuses on improving the trustworthiness and efficiency of large language models for knowledge-intensive tasks. He has served as a Senior Area Chair for ACL and an Area Chair for NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, and EMNLP. He received his bachelor's degree from IIT Kanpur and his Ph.D. from Carnegie Mellon University. His research is supported by grants from the NSF, Amazon, Procter & Gamble, Thinking Machines Labs, and the Learning Engineering Virtual Institute. He received the Amazon Research Award in 2021.

talks.speaker: Maria Antoniak
talks.title: Language Models and the Culture of Science: Adoption, Homogenization, and Policy
talks.abstract: Language models are cultural technologies; they reflect and reshape the norms of the communities that use them. They are already deeply integrated into the research workflow, but how exactly are researchers using them, and what are the consequences for scientific practice and infrastructure? In this talk, I present a series of empirical studies examining these questions from multiple angles, drawing on surveys of researchers, analyses of real chat logs, quantitative audits of papers, and interviews with interdisciplinary researchers. Together, these studies reveal measurement challenges in studying real user behavior, homogenization patterns in model outputs, and the need for policies that respect demographic and disciplinary differences.
talks.bio: I'm an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where I’m also affiliated with the Department of Information Science and a member of the Boulder NLP Group. Previously, I was a Young Investigator at the Allen Institute for AI and a postdoc at the Pioneer Centre for AI at the University of Copenhagen. I completed my PhD in Information Science at Cornell University, advised by David Mimno, and my master’s degree in Computational Linguistics at the University of Washington. I’ve also spent time at places like ETH Zürich, Microsoft Research FATE, Twitter Cortex, and Facebook Core Data Science.

talks.speaker: Michael Hanna
talks.title: Latent Planning in LLMs
talks.abstract: LLMs can often perform seemingly planning-intensive tasks, like writing coherent stories or functioning code, without explicitly verbalizing a plan; however, the extent to which they implicitly plan is unknown. In this talk, I will explore models' latent planning via feature circuits, which allow us to find causally relevant features that they use when processing their inputs; I will provide an in-depth explanation of what these are, and how they work. I will next use feature circuits to show how Qwen-3 models latently plan in simple scenarios: for example, given the input Someone who handles financial records is... larger models activate an accountant feature that causes them to output the correct indefinite article an. Finally, I will show that these models' abilities to plan over longer spans of text such as rhyming couplets is weak but increases with scale.
talks.bio: Michael Hanna is a 4th-year PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, supervised by Sandro Pezzelle and Yonatan Belinkov. His research lies at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive science, using tools such as causal interventions and circuits to uncover the mechanisms that underlie models' abilities. In past work, he has studied how GPT-2 computes the greater-than operation and found features used by models to process garden-path sentences. He is currently interested in using feature circuits to develop a unified account of how models represent and process linguistic structure across syntactic phenomena. Michael is a member of the ELLIS PhD program and is supported by an OpenAI Superalignment Fellowship.

talks.speaker: Yang Janet Liu
talks.title: Making Models Make Sense: A Discourse-Aware Take on Modeling and Evaluation
talks.abstract: Human language—and especially at the discourse level, where meanings unfold across sentences and speakers' intents—lives in the wild: many valid perspectives, many shades of interpretation. How do we decide which meaning is intended or justifiable? And when machines attempt to make sense of this variation, what enables them to understand how sentences connect together in order to generate fluent and coherent text? In this talk, I present a research program at the intersection of discourse processing, natural language generation, and variation in language understanding. I begin by examining LLMs' grasp of discourse coherence using discourse relation classification as a testbed, highlighting where they succeed and generalize and where they fail [1]. I then present a study showing how decomposing model reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought explanations) into discourse units can help explain benchmarks exhibiting label variation such as NLI and QA [2]. Lastly, I discuss variation-aware evaluation in summarization, a discourse-level NLP task, and motivate the necessity of evaluation practices that embrace variation and leverage discourse structure [3]. Together, these studies chart a path toward a discourse-grounded approach that creatively transforms established discourse theories into actionable insights for modeling and evaluation, thereby contributing to the development of more interpretable and robust models that align closely with human understanding and systems more capable of nuanced language comprehension. [1] https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.915/ (ACL 2025) [2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23368 (EMNLP 2025) [3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14335 (INLG 2025)
talks.bio: Dr. Liu is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Linguistics at the University of Pittsburgh. Previously, she was a Postdoctoral Researcher at the MaiNLP research lab at the Center for Information and Language Processing (CIS) at LMU Munich, led by Prof. Dr. Barbara Plank, and was affiliated with the Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML). She earned her Ph.D. in Computational Linguistics from the Department of Linguistics at Georgetown University, where she was advised by Amir Zeldes, Ph.D., and was a member of Corpling@GU and Computational Linguistics @ Georgetown (GUCL). She was also a student research affiliate of NERT, directed by Nathan Schneider, Ph.D.

talks.speaker: Bryan Li
talks.title: Towards Multilingual Evaluations of Knowledge for Large Language Models
talks.abstract: Despite significant progress in multilingual benchmarks, the usefulness of contemporary language models (LMs) outside of English remains limited. This is due in large part to limited prior assessments, which have left under-studied how LMs perform on tasks which require multilingual knowledge --- information, facts, and principles. Notably, real-world knowledge across languages is not just translated; it is distributed differently and can even conflict. In this thesis, I develop benchmarks and methods to assess LMs' ability to handle knowledge across languages. I first study the parametric knowledge of LMs through two multilingual benchmarks on complex reasoning and on geopolitics. By varying the language an underlying query is specified in, these tasks reveal that LMs respond inconsistently, showing their struggle with transferring knowledge learned in one language to others. I formalize this issue through the notion of cross-lingual robustness in three aspects. I further show that informed strategies, such as program code and prompting cues, can bridge the knowledge gap between languages and elicit more robust responses. A popular paradigm to address shortcomings of LM's static knowledge is through retrieval-augmented LMs (RALMs), which incorporate retrieval over external resources. However, multilingual retrieval warrants careful consideration of how knowledge across languages is discrete and distinct. The second part of this thesis investigates how LMs interact with contextual knowledge, which is retrieved from external resources. Experimentation focuses on the composition of retrieval databases, from language to provenance. I find that current LMs are able to utilize multilingual and multi-source retrieval and general more cross-lingually robust responses. These findings have implications for not only multilingual abilities of LMs, but also for their general knowledge abilities. However, as I show the effectiveness of proper design of multilingual tasks and contexts, my work highlights future avenues towards LM systems which can navigate, and assist users in navigating, the rich, often-conflicting streams of multilingual and multi-source information.
talks.bio: Bryan Li is a final-year PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania, advised by Prof. Chris Callison-Burch. His research focuses on multilingual evaluations for large language models, spanning both the fields of natural language processing and computational social science. His work has appeared in conferences such as ACL, NAACL, ICLR, and EMNLP. Outside of research, you can find him in a trendy cafe, a river-side running trail, or at a concert hall.

talks.speaker: Ahmed Elhady
talks.title: Emergent Abilities of LLMs under Continued Pretraining for Language Adaptation
talks.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong results in multilingual tasks, yet emergent abilities are dominated by English and a few high-resource languages, while (low) resource languages lag behind. Attributing this to the unbalanced distribution of training data, Continued Pretraining (CPT) is often used to address this gap, but English typically plays a central role in that process. We examine the impact of English in CPT and challenge assumptions about the training dynamics causing emergent abilities in multilingual adaptation.
talks.bio: My name is Ahmed Salem Mohamed Elhady...or just Salem. I am a PhD Research Student at the University of the Basque Country (UPV/EHU) under the supervision of Mikel Artetxe and Eneko Agirre. We are working on analysing and improving multi-lingual capabilities in LLMs, with a focus on reasoning. Before the PhD, I worked as NLP Engineer at Microsoft Bing News's Trust and Safety, and at Implicit.ai: a Microsoft-backed startup working on enterprise data summarization and search
